title: An unmanageable club? Carrick the latest to suffer in Manchester United’s faded grandeur
author: John Brewin
text:
Only Matt Busby and Alex Ferguson have truly succeeded in the Old Trafford hot seat with each casting uneasy shadows

S hould any football club fit the Great Man theory of history it is Manchester United . In the past 100 years, only Matt Busby and Alex Ferguson have knocked the club into shape. A pair of 20th-century Scotsmen, born 15 miles apart in Bellshill and Govan respectively, found the key. Otherwise, United has been a managerial dustbin, Michael Carrick the latest likely lobbed on the pile.

Busby and Ferguson built the club around themselves, possessing the charisma to convince others that theirs was the path to follow. Carrick, an insider, a club man, is falling victim to the same isolation as his predecessors in failure . Bruno Fernandes and Lisandro Martínez going off-piste in TV interviews to depth charge Carrick were actually following club tradition. With glamour comes decadence, the faded grandeur that has so often chased a United manager out the door.

Beyond Busby and Ferguson, each United manager who also served felt the lash of desperation of a falling giant. Each of their defenestrations has featured an infighting that would not have been out of place in ancient Rome. Favouritism, nepotism, self-interest, entitlement, complacency and sentimentality have been the betrayal of a legend, to use the title of Michael Crick’s and David Smith’s “ j’accuse ” book from 1989. Living with the legend and influence of those two managers leads the list of difficulties.

United fans know such history too well. “You lousy bastards, you let him down,” Brian Kidd told teammates when the bullet came for Wilf McGuinness, Busby’s immediate successor, in December 1970. Busby himself had done the deed. A December 1972 meeting at Selhurst Park with Tommy Docherty as Crystal Palace beat United 5-0 hastened the end for Frank O’Farrell.

Docherty’s turn came. His sacking in 1977 after an affair with the physio’s wife was announced by the club secretary, Les Olive, from behind the oak door of the chairman Louis Edwards’ Cheshire mansion. Dave Sexton was sacked in 1981 despite winning his last seven matches. Falling attendances at “Cold Trafford” did for “Whispering Dave”. Ron Atkinson turned his November 1986 sacking into a party in the office that also housed the club sunbed. Big Ron’s parting gift was the hangovers that greeted Ferguson’s first day in charge.

Ferguson’s predecessors had been intimidated by the fog of pipe smoke wafting down Old Trafford’s corridors. O’Farrell had needed to ask Busby if the former manager could vacate the manager’s office. “A fantasy world” is how O’Farrell described Busby’s coterie of gossipy former players who teed off with “the old man” at Davyhulme golf course. “There was no reality in the myth,” the Corkman dubbed “O’Failure” said in 1991.

Busby’s indulgence of George Best, careering towards oblivion, created problems O’Farrell found unsolvable. Docherty showed the political wiles to jettison Best in January 1974 but also shelling Bobby Charlton, Denis Law and Paddy Crerand created enemies. Falling in love with Mary Brown, with whom Docherty remained for the rest of his life, was enough for a boardroom moral majority to rid themselves of their turbulent manager.

Ferguson’s successors must deal with his continued presence, the face in the crowd photographers and TV directors seek. His patronage of Malcolm Glazer’s 2005 takeover is a dubious legacy dragging down those who have followed him. Ferguson mostly keeps his own counsel, a well-remunerated club ambassador until Sir Jim Ratcliffe cancelled a £2m annual stipen d in 2024. There have been slips. “You should always start with your best players,” Ferguson told the mixed martial arts fighter Khabib Nurmagomedov in 2021 when Ole Gunnar Solskjær had dropped Cristiano Ronaldo , loose talk escaping to social media.

Ferguson’s part in Ronaldo’s disastrous return to Old Trafford evidenced continuing back-channel influence, echoing Busby and Best. Carrick, during his press conference last Friday, mentioned his chats with his former boss. The omission of Fernandes for the Bournemouth game , left to sulk on the bench in club tracksuit, was classic Fergie politics.

A Ferguson facsimile is a fool’s errand. Carrick might have learned the lessons dished out to Solskjær, to whom he was assistant. After refusing to use Ferguson’s parking space and misty-eyed chat of “the boss”, nobody was buying the affable, gentle Norwegian cosplaying as a Glaswegian hard man.

Not that an injection of the alpha male has been much more use. Time has been kinder to the Louis van Gaal and José Mourinho regimes as subsequent failures pile up, but both failed to embrace the expectations of attacking football.

Not that other club traditions were avoided. The subterfuge that brought in Mourinho was as dastardly as any of the post-Busby knifings. “People know him as a larger-than-life character,” the executive vice-chairman Ed Woodward said on Van Gaal’s 2014 appointment. “My wife had to find out when she was in the lift with Woodward’s family,” Van Gaal said of finding, in the haze of celebrating the 2016 FA Cup final victory, that he was being replaced . His former Barcelona assistant had successfully lobbied Woodward. Attempts have been made by the Glazers’ operatives and, since December 2023, Ratcliffe’s Ineos, to corporatise and professionalise but United’s innate excess and anarchy keeps overtaking rationale.

Using the means of a Netflix special, Mourinho has retrofitted his part in the story, he and Ferguson revealing together the fact he turned United down in 2013 . The inference is that if Mourinho had arrived then all would have been roses. It is an unconvincing attempt at airbrushing both men’s reputations. Where does that leave David Moyes, the immediate successor painted as afterthought? In July 2013, Ferguson was celebrated as kingmaker, Moyes the rightful heir.…

title: Lucinda Brand switches to Canyon-SRAM for the next two years with plans to end road cycling career at Paris-Roubaix
author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
text:
An "exciting new chapter" for multi-talented Lucinda Brand has been sealed with a two-year contract and a dual rule with Canyon-SRAM Scalable Capital for 2027. She has spent nearly half of her 18 years in the pro peloton with Lidl-Trek and will continue on the Women's WorldTour level through 2028 at her new home.

"It was almost like a new fire had been lit inside me," she said in a press release about her decision being based on more than a change of team.

"I didn’t want this to be just one more year on the bike. I wanted it to be the beginning of a longer-term project, where I could keep contributing to the sport and build on what I’ve already done as a rider. I really feel that this team shares my passion, ambition and philosophy on cycling, which gives me a lot of energy and motivation for this next chapter, and for what we can create together."

The 37-year-old Dutch rider will join as a rider, targeting stage races and one-day races through to Paris-Roubaix Femmes in 2028, where a finish in the velodrome is planned to be a career finale. Then she will transition to a staff role for the German-based WorldTour squad.

"When the opportunity came along to potentially finish my road cycling career at Paris-Roubaix, I knew straight away that it was a chance I had to grab with both hands," she said.

"Over the last few years, I’ve noticed that my role as a rider has become more than just racing. In a way, I’ve already been taking on the responsibilities that a sports director might have, and I’ve discovered how much I enjoy that side of the sport.

"I really love working with young, ambitious athletes, sharing my experience, and helping them grow. It’s something I’d love to explore further and develop myself in. That’s why it was important for me to find a team that recognised those qualities and was willing to give me an opportunity to grow in that direction."

Canyon-SRAM adds new title sponsor Scalable Capital next year and the roster features half of the riders at 24 years old or younger, including 19-year-old Emily DIxon moving up form the development team. The team's Director of Sport Rolf Aldag said Brand was an "obvious choice" as a veteran to help the team grow.

"There are a lot of changes happening to our roster, and we’ll have quite a few younger riders, so we need to create the right mix of potential versus experience and leadership," Aldag said.

"Having Lucinda is as much about leadership as it is mentorship. But, it’s not all about race results, it’s also how she also lives and pays attention to all the smaller details that are critical for reaching the very top.

"So, I think she can mentor our younger riders really well, and then bring a lot of stability to the classics team, which is a strong sporting focus for the next two years. We believe that the addition of Lucinda will be a real game-changer for us.”

Brand began her career as a 19-year-old with a Dutch squad and moved to the powerful Rabobank-Liv team from 2013 to 2016, racing during that time with compatriots Marianne Vos, Anna van der Breggen, and Annemiek van Vleuten. After winning the Dutch elite women's road race ahead of her teammates that first year then winning GP de Plouay-Bretagne in 2014, her road career ignited the next season with four stage podiums, including two victories, at Giro d'Italia for women and a second Dutch road title.

The team structure at Canyon-SRAM, with a singular focus on women's cycling, was one of the great appeals to make this transition.

"I’ve spent the last years in a very big organisation, with different teams all under one roof, and that has been a great experience. But, I’m really excited about coming into a smaller environment, where the lines are shorter, communication is more direct, and everyone is working towards the same goal. What I really like is that Canyon-SRAM still has a whole pathway – from development to the pro team – but within an organisation that is fully built for women’s cycling," she added.

On the road she has amassed 28 victories, including Baloise Ladies Tour, Tour de Suisse Women, and Thüringen Ladies Tour while at Lidl-Trek. This year she competed at the Giro d'Italia Women for a 15th time, challenging from a breakaway to go second on stage 2 into Salice Terme.

She's had podiums at the most challenging one-day races - Dwars door Vlaanderen, Amstel Gold Race, Liège-Bastogne-Liège and Paris-Roubaix. And it was the cobbles of 'Hell of the North' where she wanted to leave her mark for road racing.

“I love the challenge, the way the race unfolds, and the toughness of the cobbles – riding over them is unique and not something everyone can do," she said about the 'Hell of the North', where she was third in 2022 and 10th in 2026.

"For me, Paris-Roubaix is the race where road cycling and cyclocross come together in a beautiful way. Every time I think about racing it, my heart beats just that little bit faster.”

This time of year Brand goes back to work on her highly-decorated cyclo-cross duties, where she begins a 10th season with a team directed by Sven Nys. On the volatile tracks that range from sand to dirt to mud, Brand has 77 career victories. She attributed Nys with helping her connect with Trek-Segafredo years ago to give her a renewed interest in top-level road racing.

"When I was losing my joy for cycling, Sven brought it back. His passion, energy and belief in me made me fall in love with the sport all over again," she wrote on Instagram, adding that she would "always look back on with a big smile and so much gratitude" as she moves on to her new chapter.

She recently extended her off-road commitment to Baloise Verzekeringen - Het Poetsbureau Lions squad for this season and the 2027-2028 CX campaign. She opened this season with five podiums, including wins on the first two rounds of HG Cross series and the Superprestige series opener in Overijse . Last year she won the UCI Cyclo-cross World Championships a second time and also won the UCI World Cup and X2O Badkamers Trofee series.

title: Man Utd stick with Carrick - inside a turbulent 48 hours at Old Trafford
text:
When Michael Carrick disappeared down the tunnel after Manchester United's loss to Bournemouth at Old Trafford on Sunday, the support from fans for a legendary player turned to hostility and anger at the current squad.

The atmosphere afterwards was said to be emotional.

Carrick was the last to leave the stadium and, as usual, patiently posed for selfies and signed shirts for the fans who remained on what had been a foul day weather-wise, and an awful one on the pitch.

Asked in his post-match news conference if he expected to be in charge for Saturday's trip to Chelsea, Carrick said: "I'm not expecting anything in particular, to be honest. I'm carrying on as normal."

Few felt that was sustainable. Even Carrick's coaching team wondered whether they would survive.

United have decided Carrick and his players will have the chance to turn the present situation around. No timescale has been put on this, but Carrick will be in charge at Chelsea, with his team 16th in the table.

They have a crucial Champions League match against Roma three days later, then a Premier League encounter with in-form Aston Villa before a two-week international break.

No-one from Manchester United is saying so, but that would be the most obvious time to decide if a change of coach is required.

On Monday morning, when it was widely anticipated an announcement terminating Carrick's tenure would be made, a senior figure at United said calmness and a clear head would be needed to navigate the turbulence around Old Trafford.

Carrick had been treading water since the crushing 4-1 defeat at Como on 21 October - one of the worst European nights in club history.

Respected United fan and United We Stand fanzine editor Andy Mitten, who interviewed chief executive Omar Berrada on behalf of the club last June, described the performance as "an affront to the name of Manchester United".

In addition to the catastrophic nature of the performance, captain Bruno Fernandes publicly questioned Carrick's tactics and the inability of his coaches to spot what was going wrong.

Fernandes' comments came a week after defender Lisandro Martinez said he had expected more investment in the squad and - turning attention to Jason Wilcox - "more from our technical director".

It painted a picture of a squad out of control, posing an immediate dilemma for the United hierarchy.

Feeling it would look reactionary and impulsive to remove Carrick based on the negativity of one game, United stuck with the 45-year-old for the Bournemouth match - only for that to turn sour thanks to a performance that, arguably, was worse than the one in Italy.

Fernandes played no part and was dropped to the bench. Afterwards, the Portugal star liked an Instagram post which included the caption: "Never push a loyal person to the point where they no longer care".

Late on Sunday night, BBC Sport was led to believe a final decision to sack Carrick had not been made, and the judgement would stretch into Monday.

There was no decision then, either. The United players who started against Bournemouth were given the day off but bizarrely, Fernandes and Carrick were both at Carrington. Fernandes was having pre-planned treatment while Carrick watched a closed doors Under-21s game.

Also at the training ground were Berrada and Wilcox, discussing what the immediate future should look like. Sources say it is inconceivable minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the Glazer family would not have been part of those discussions.

It was early evening before it became clear there would be no update on Carrick's future. His arrival at Carrington at 07:30 GMT on Tuesday was a sign he would take training as normal and, along with Fernandes and several other players, Carrick signed autographs and posed for photographs with a group of fans invited to the training ground that day.

Four hours later, United sources confirmed he would be in charge at Stamford Bridge.

The current predicament at the club is seen as not being entirely Carrick's fault.

Senior figures at the club feel United's players - a squad they think are capable of qualifying for the Champions League - are underperforming badly and should shoulder some of the blame.

There does seem to be a general desire to help Carrick out. One player told BBC Sport: "The feeling is that we all want to put it right. Players, staff, everyone."

It is not known if the "we" includes Fernandes, and BBC Sport has not been made aware of what, if any, conversations have taken place between the captain and his boss.

Obviously, it is easier to get rid of one manager and his backroom team than an entire squad of players - and if results do not turn around, Carrick will pay the price.

One former senior United official told BBC Sport: "Ordinarily, Michael would have gone. The last two performances were unacceptable and team discipline is broken. Not doing it is fascinating and risky."

Cynics may argue the main reason Carrick is still in a job is because of the inability to secure a replacement before the Chelsea game. Additionally, some of the coaches current Under-18s boss Darren Fletcher called on to help him during his spell as interim manager in January are now part of the senior set-up.

As highlighted by BBC Sport on Monday, Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann were among the options explored by United as they weighed up whether to make a change. Any decision to appoint Howe would trigger a multi-million pound compensation payment from his former club Newcastle.

BBC Sport has also been told former Chelsea boss Antonio Conte is willing to have a conversation about the job, although there has been no direct contact.

That trio are all out of work - as is Kieran McKenna, who worked with Carrick as part of Ole Gunnar Solskjaer's coaching team at United and then left for Ipswich.

Aston Villa's Unai Emery also has strong backing at United, but the club are realistic about their chances of tempting the Spaniard from Villa Park.…

title: More Chinese brands in the pro peloton for 2027 as TotalEnergies swaps Cube for Pardus
author: thomas.wieckowski@futurenet.com (Tom Wieckowski)
text:
Team TotalEnergies has announced a new bike sponsor today in the form of the Chinese brand Pardus.

The two parties have announced a three-year partnership which will run from 2027 through to 2029.

In an Instagram announcement, they spoke of a 'strategic partnership based on technological innovation.'

This is the second bike sponsor announcement in recent weeks after Specialized and Soudal-Quick-Step parted ways after a long and successful partnership together. Incidentally, Total Energies raced on Specialized bikes prior to partnering with Enve.

The team also released a press release on its website containing a little more information. Pardus will become a 'material sponsor' for all of the team's squads, which include the UCI Pro Team and U19 and U23 squads.

Pardus bikes are raced by the Chinese National Team and were also used by Team Vini Fantini in 2025 at a high level in races like the UAE Tour.

The Total Energies teams will use the SPK EVO G4 and Robin EVO G3 road models, along with the Gomera Evo TT bike.

Those are models that may not be as familiar as those from more established brands, and Pardus represents another Chinese brand joining cycling's top flight. Although Total Energies is not a WorldTour team, they will be riding some of the world's biggest races on Pardus machines over the next three years.

"Working alongside the Chinese national team since the Rio Olympics, we have gained in-depth knowledge of the demands of elite competition and the expectations of riders.

"This partnership will be a fantastic opportunity to share our technical expertise throughout the season, continuously enhance our product ranges through interaction with athletes, and solidify Pardus' presence at the heart of European cycling culture," said Terry Gong, Deputy General Manager of Pardus.

The brand's aero model is the SPKG4 Evo (pictured below). This is the model we may well see the TotalEnergies riders racing on most of the time.

The best indoor cycling accessories for under £25 / $25
author: Tim Perkin
text:
Indoor cycling has significantly grown in popularity, offering riders the possibility to train year-round regardless of the weather or daylight. Creating a comfortable and effective indoor training environment can improve your experience.

Improving your setup doesn’t have to be expensive, with some of the most valuable additions being the simplest and cheapest.

A few well-chosen accessories can help you stay hydrated, manage sweat, protect your bike, and ride more comfortably, all without stretching your budget.

If you are looking to make a small investment to make your indoor training more enjoyable, here are five affordable accessories, priced under £25 / $25, that deliver practical benefits and are good value for money.

You don't need to buy everything at once, either. Start with the essentials and add to your setup as needed.

A water bottle is one of the first accessories every cyclist should buy, as indoor cycling is thirsty work!

Although bottles are relatively inexpensive, investing in one or two durable options is worthwhile, particularly during the indoor training season when you'll use them regularly.

Elite supplies nearly every WorldTour cycling team in the professional peloton with bottles, so they know a thing or two about them.

Elite’s Fly Tex bottle is one of the most-used bottles in cycling, so this would be my recommendation. It's made from recyclable materials and is BPA-free.

They come in multiple colours and three different sizes: 950 ml, 750 ml, and 550 ml.

Depending on your selection, prices start at $11.99, so for $25 you could buy a couple.

A towel is an essential accessory, as indoor cycling is a sweaty business. Fortunately, Elite has designed one that is fit for purpose. Measuring 1,300 x 300 mm and made from 100% natural cotton, it is a practical size to hang around your neck or drape over your handlebars.

Compact and soft, it's a practical addition to any indoor training setup, helping you manage sweat throughout your session.

A front wheel riser block is a simple accessory that can make indoor training more comfortable.

Placed beneath your bike's front wheel when using a compatible wheel-on or direct-drive trainer setup, it helps level the bike and provides a more stable riding position.

Riser blocks are available from numerous brands and are generally inexpensive. With prices starting at around $8.99, it's an affordable way to improve your indoor cycling setup.

Whilst you can use household objects to do the same job, they can be prone to moving under effort. A riser block is simply the best tool for the job.

Before buying, check that the block is compatible with your trainer and front-wheel setup, especially if you are running gravel tyres.

Muc-Off is renowned for its cleaning products. Its Sweat Protect spray is designed to help protect bike components from corrosion associated with sweat exposure.

Using a suitable protective product can help reduce the risk of corrosion and keep your bike in better condition over time.

If you want to safeguard your bike from the potential damage caused by heavy indoor use, this is a worthwhile investment. Always follow the manufacturer's instructions and check product compatibility before applying it.

Sweat can take a toll on your bike over time, particularly when it repeatedly drips onto the handlebars, frame, and components during indoor training.

The Wahoo Fitness Sweat Guard sits across your handlebars and attaches around the back of your saddle. It helps shield your bike from perspiration by catching sweat before it drips onto the frame and other components, where prolonged exposure can contribute to corrosion.

There are multiple brands on the market that sell these, but we like the Wahoo Fitness Sweat Guard.

title: Simpler, cheaper hybrid V8s proposed for next F1 rules
text:
Formula 1's next engine regulations are set to introduce V8 turbo hybrid engines that are simplified and less expensive to make compared to the existing rules.

A proposal document sent by governing body the FIA to the six manufacturers in F1 outlines a framework for discussions on engines to be introduced in either 2030 or 2031.

Multiple sources within F1 have provided BBC Sport with the details within the document.

The plan, which comes after initial discussions with individual engine manufacturers on a one-to-one basis, proposes cheaper, lighter, simpler engines with a more visceral sound.

However, the FIA has moved away from its initial proposal to return to naturally aspirated engines.

The stated aim of the new rules is to introduce lighter, more responsive cars, increased emphasis on driver skill, relevant technologies, reduced cost, to make it easier for new manufacturers to enter F1 and to continue with the sport's commitment to reducing emissions.

This comes after criticism of the new engines introduced this year for their complexity and the way their design and operation has diminished the driving challenge of some of F1's best corners.

Will F1 go back to the future with its engines?

The engines used in F1 at the moment are 1.6-litre V6 turbos with a power split of 53-47 between the internal combustion engine and electrical components. This will be changed to 60-40 in two steps by 2028.

The FIA document proposes a V8 engine with a capacity of between 2-2.3-litres with a smaller turbo running at reduced boost pressure and a less powerful hybrid system.

The electrical motor would have a recovery capacity of 200kW compared to the current 350kW.

The idea is for 100kW (134bhp) of this to be available at all times, with a further 100kW to be used for a push-to-pass or overtake mode.

The rest of the total power output of in the region of 900bhp will be provided by the internal combustion engine.

F1 will continue with fully sustainable fuels but with the ambition to make the requirements around them less complex and therefore lower production costs.

The aim is to cut a total of 80kg from the overall weight of the cars.

The proposal changes the previous stance of the FIA on naturally aspirated engines - president Mohammed Ben Sulayem initially proposed a return of V10s at the start of last year and has more recently been pushing V8s.

The addition of the turbo satisfies the need for the engines to be road-relevant, as well as increasing efficiency and requiring less fuel than a pure naturally aspirated engine.

The published proposals can be seen as a kind of middle ground between Ben Sulayem's initial stance, the desire of at least some manufacturers to keep turbos and a significant hybrid element, and a recognition that the latest rules were flawed in concept and execution.

The new engines will have none of the problems of energy starvation about which drivers have complained this season.

Fernando Alonso has called F1 the "battery world championship" and described fast corners as "the charging station for the car", while Max Verstappen has described the new rules as "Formula E on steroids" and anti-racing.

Both have since tempered their criticisms having seen that the sport's bosses have listened to their comments on the engines and made immediate changes to the rules this year as well as started working towards a new direction in the future.

The fundamental framework of the proposal for the new engine's architecture is said to be basically acceptable to all the manufacturers.

However, the details around how the rules operate will need discussion.

The document outlines two possible ways forward for the new rule set.

One is aimed at minimising necessary adaptation - for example, a 2.1-litre V8 could be produced by simply adding two cylinders to the current 1.6-litre blocks and reducing the size of the turbo and MGU-K (hybrid motor).

The other, more controversial, is to have an external manufacturer design and supply a baseline power-unit with a high degree of standardisation, on to which manufacturers could add a degree of customisation.

However, insiders say the manufacturers are all aligned on wanting to design and build their own power-units and for engines to remain a performance differentiator.

The companies who currently supply engines to F1 teams are Mercedes, Ferrari, Audi, Honda and Red Bull. Cadillac, which entered F1 this year with its own team, is planning to produce an engine to the new rules.

There are two further arguments to steer away from the standardisation route:

The first is that the reasons for it - to safeguard against manufacturers leaving the sport - is irrelevant as all six will be committed under the new rule set.

The second is that the standardisation of electronics control units this season has led to a series of problems, such as at the start of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia when cars were restricted to not much more than walking pace because of a software bug.

The document outlines a proposal to cut the engine budget cap by 50% from the current level of $190m (£143m) per year.

However, this is considered a starting point for discussions, while there are also concerns about providing a suitable glide path down to the new number to enable teams to manage the impact on workforces.

Discussions around the budget cap also involve the need to balance ongoing development of the existing engines with design and construction of the new ones.

That topic is interlinked with whether the new rules will come into force in 2030 or 2031.

The existing contracts in F1 bind the FIA, teams and commercial rights holder together only until 2030.

Ben Sulayem has previously threatened to introduce his own rules unilaterally in 2031.

That threat appears to have receded and the process has been marked by a spirit of co-operation, which is expected to continue.…

title: Zwift racing this winter? Then the Wahoo Kickr V6 is our best choice smart trainer for grabbing those virtual bragging rights – it's currently got a rarely seen discount at Tredz
author: paul.brett@futurenet.com (Paul Brett)
text:
It's indoor cycling week here at , and our experts will be bringing a week of indoor-riding advice and features, from the best cycling apps to buying advice on the best smart trainers .

The Wahoo Kickr V6 is undoubtedly one of the most impressive and expensive indoor smart trainers on the market. It holds the title of the best smart trainer for racing, and just narrowly missed out on the best overall to its more budget-friendly Wahoo Kickr Core 2 sibling.

If you're gearing up for indoor riding, you won't go wrong with either of these Wahoo offerings. However, if you want to take your indoor riding beyond fitness and casual spins, the Wahoo Kickr V6 takes things up a level, with an all-new Race Mode which uses WiFi capability to broadcast power up to 10x faster.

As well as seamless connectivity, this Wahoo Kickr deal is paired with the equally impressive Zwift Click and Cog virtual shifting system, perfect for Zwift racing. The Cog and Click is considered a significant tactical advantage, as virtual shifting changes resistance electronically at the trainer flywheel without moving the physical chain. So no risk of dropped chains, loud crunching, or hesitation that can come with a standard cassette when dumping gears during a sprint.

TheWahoo Kickr V6, equipped with the Zwift Cog and Click system, has hit the lowest price we've seen this year, and at this price, there isn't much to say other than if you're in the market for one of the best smart trainers, then this is an excellent purchase.

It performs incredibly well with +/- 1% power accuracy, excellent ride feel, and comprehensive connectivity, meaning it's a superb way to enjoy indoor training.

title: Vollering Betters Pogačar with Near-Perfect Season and More Hot Takes from the Year-End Rankings
author: Jim Cotton
text:
Demi Vollering just wrapped up the greatest season in the pro peloton.

The Dutchwoman obliterated the women’s UCI rankings with a season-long rout that won her the Giro d’Italia, Tour de France, road world championships, and a whole lot more.

Vollering topped the 2026 year-end rankings with a haul of 9,330 UCI points – some 65 percent more than second-place Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney. Vollering’s Polish nemesis finished the year on 5,660 points.

Spanish super talent Paula Blasi rounded out her breakout season third in the rankings with 5,201 points.

Vollering’s season wasn’t only the best in the women’s road peloton.

It was more impressive than anything achieved on the men’s side of the sport, too.

This year, Vollering strung together a 2026 season even more dominant than Tadej Pogačar’s.

Yes, the Slovenian won the Tour de France for a record-breaking fifth time, unlocked Milan-San Remo, and topped the UCI league by echelons, despite racing for only six months.

He probably would have also won the Vuelta, worlds, and Il Lombardia if a brutal crash didn’t prematurely end his season.

Vollering won two monuments, the world and European titles, and topped the GC of every stage-race she started.

The 29-year-old became only the second woman after Annemiek van Vleuten to complete the triple crown.

And she hit the podium of every one-day road race she started bar Strade Bianche. Being directed off course (depending on your reading of the situation) at the sterrato classic will do that to one’s podium aspirations, we guess.

Vollering’s 2026 season was a masterpiece on-par with anything that GOATs like Van Vleuten, Anna van der Breggen, or Marianne Vos have put together. It was a Hall of Fame eight months that saw FDJ Suez’s superstar leader amass more UCI points than eight women’s WorldTour teams.

Dem Vollering: Rider of the year. Gotta be .

The 2026 UCI rider and team rankings, and a ranking of rider victories, can be found at the bottom of this post.

Here is our breakdown and hot takes from the 2026 men’s rankings.

One thing Vollering didn’t do this year?

But we’ll let her off. Super-mega sprinter Lorena Wiebes was in her own orbit , again.

With a total of 24 victories, Wiebes won the most for the third year in a row. Not even a controversial bike weight disqualification at the Giro d’Italia slowed the 27-year-old’s High Speed Express.

Vollering ranked second in individual wins with 16.

The extent of Wiebes’ and Vollering’s dominance over the Women’s WorldTour is brutally clear if you scan further down the year end victory table.

With “only” 8 and 7 wins apiece, some might think Marlen Reusser and Blasi in third and fourth were riding with brake rub.

Picnic-PostNL’s troubles are not isolated to the men’s peloton.

The under-scrutiny Dutch team is dead-last in the Women’s WorldTour rankings with a total of 2,450 points. That’s 11 percent of the most successful team, UAE L’Imad. The news that long-time leader Pfeiffer Georgi is headed for the exit door will compound Picnic-PostNL’s problems in 2027.

Speaking of UAE l’Imad – the Women’s WorldTour got a new superteam in 2026.

The UAE-based squad topped the UCI charts for the first time courtesy of its prolific leadership trident Blasi, Elisa Longo Borghini, and Dominika Wlodarczyk.

Former dominators FDJ United-Suez and SD Worx-ProTime went two-three, respectively.

But getting to the top ain’t the same as staying at the top.

UAE L’Imad’s winning season might be a one-and-done. Blasi’s blockbuster move to Movistar will blow a hole in her former UAE team in 2027.

Last up – take a look at the rankings again.

Pauline Ferrand-Prévot has bombed out of the top 20 after her incredible 2025 season. PFP was woman of the year in 2025 after she won both Paris-Roubaix and the Tour de France femmes.

This year, the template that had worked so well for the Frenchwoman went very wrong, and her form nosedived soon after spring.

Ferrand-Prévot’s year-end ranking of 31st says a lot about her annus horribilis.

But it might not paint the fairest picture.

PFP wasn’t near the top of the board in 2025, either. The 34-year-old races so selectively that she finished only 13th in 2025.

Ferrand-Prévot doesn’t care about points, she cares about history and legacy. 2026 was no doubt a season she’ll be hoping gets lost in the mists of time.

Carrick given chance to save job as he stays for Manchester United’s game at Chelsea
author: Jamie Jackson
text:
Jason Wilcox has driven decision to stand by head coach

United would have to pay Newcastle about £3m for Howe

Michael Carrick has been given the chance to save his job by turning Manchester United’s results around, with the head coach remaining in place for Saturday’s visit to Chelsea.

The decision by Jason Wilcox, the director of football, and Omar Berrada, the chief executive, can be viewed as a surprise given United’s dire form.

Sunday’s abject 3-0 league home defeat by Bournemouth followed Wednesday’s equally dire 4-1 reverse at Como in the Champions League.

Carrick’s side have won twice in 12 games and were eliminated from the Carabao Cup by Brighton. United are 16th in the Premier League, a point above the relegation zone.

Yet Wilcox, who has driven the retaining of Carrick, wants to give the 45-year-old a chance to transform form and results. Whether Carrick could survive another poor performance and result at Stamford Bridge is in the balance.

United host Roma in the Champions League three days later, then Aston Villa in the league the following Saturday. Carrick’s reprieve may also be a move to allow time for Wilcox to secure a replacement should the decision be taken to sack him.

United will have to pay Newcastle about £3m in compensation if they want Eddie Howe. He is Wilcox’s prime candidate if a change is made and wants the job. When he left Newcastle in July a deal was struck on the remaining terms of his contract which means the club would be due compensation.

United would also have to pay Newcastle a minor sum for Howe’s staff, headed by his assistant, Jason Tindall.

Manchester United’s director of recruitment, Christopher Vivell, has been pushing the case of Julian Nagelsmann, the former Germany and Bayern Munich head coach.

title: Carrick to stay in charge of Man Utd for Chelsea game
text:
Michael Carrick will remain in charge of Manchester United for their trip to Chelsea this weekend.

Sources have told BBC Sport that the 45-year-old will be given the opportunity to turn things around at Old Trafford following a dismal start to the campaign.

Carrick oversaw training on Tuesday morning, as United look to end a run of eight matches without a win in all competitions when they visit Stamford Bridge on Saturday.

Sunday's 3-0 defeat by Bournemouth at Old Trafford plunged Carrick's future into doubt, with United sitting one place above the relegation zone.

It is understood United's hierarchy have explored the possibility of replacing Carrick, with ex-Newcastle United boss Eddie Howe and former Germany head coach Julian Nagelsmann under consideration.

But sources have told BBC Sport that the former Middlesbrough manager will not only take charge against Chelsea but will also be given a chance to revive the club's fortunes on the pitch.

Carrick took interim charge in January following Ruben Amorim's departure and he was rewarded with the permanent job in May after securing Champions League qualification with an impressive run that resulted in them finishing third.

But United's form has collapsed this term, with Carrick's side winning just one of their eight Premier League matches so far this season.

Defender Lisandro Martinez criticised the club's board for a lack of investment following United's 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid in the Champions League earlier this month.

Captain Bruno Fernandes then took aim at Carrick's tactics following a humiliating 4-1 loss against Como in their next Champions League fixture.

The Portuguese was dropped to the bench for Sunday's loss to Bournemouth, and remained an unused substitute.

United supporters chanted Carrick's name as the former England international made his way to the tunnel after the match, but quickly directed boos at the players once Carrick had made his way off the pitch.

Carrick gestured towards the Stretford End as they chanted his name after the match.

"It wasn't a farewell from me," Carrick said on Sky Sports.

"I've mixed emotions, I'm feeling it for my players, they're going through a tough spell. Some of it we can help, some of it the situation unravels and the boys are feeling it at the moment.

"Mixed emotions for the supporters to respond in that way. To have that connection with the supporters it's mixed emotions, it'll take a bit of time to digest but I certainly appreciate their support.

"The situation is where we are and we haven't had results or performances that have been good enough."

Carrick was at also United's training ground on Monday morning, despite the first team being given the day off.

Director of football Jason Wilcox and chief executive Omar Berrada were both pictured arriving at the club's training ground on Monday, with Carrick leaving at about 17:00 GMT.

Howe, 48, is available after leaving Newcastle United last summer but any club that hires the Englishman will have to pay a multi-million pound compensation package to the Magpies after he resigned from his post with three years remaining on his deal.

Nagelsmann, 39, resigned as Germany boss following their quarter-final exit at the 2026 World Cup and is aware of United's interest in him.

Sources have also indicated Aston Villa boss Unai Emery is admired at United, but the fact he is under contract would complicate any move for the Spaniard.

Manchester United might be trying to pass this off as business as usual but the reality is anything but.

The mere fact there was no clarification around Carrick's future on Monday - both before and after he was at the training ground to watch an Under-21 game his son Jacey was part of, or on Tuesday after his 07:30 arrival at Carrington and the 11:00 training start time, fuels theories and speculation, which just adds to the air of uncertainty.

Carrick will be in charge at Stamford Bridge, but what about Roma in the Champions League on Tuesday and Aston Villa after that?

Given the woeful nature of their last two performances, how will United's players respond at Chelsea when the spotlight on them is so fierce? Can Carrick drag a performance out of them? Has he made his peace with skipper Bruno Fernandes?

Is director of football Jason Wilcox safe? There are still so many unanswered questions.

Last season's win at Stamford Bridge was one of the key results in securing Carrick the head coach's job permanently. Will the next trip there be the start of a brighter future or mark the end of his tenure?

title: Abus Hyp-E helmet review: An urban e-bike helmet that's ready for anything
author: Simon Lock
text:
572g / 20.2oz (size M tested)

S, (51-55) M (54-58), L (57-61cm)

Signal Yellow, Champagne Gold, Volcano Titan, Gleam Silver, Jungle Green

2 hours on constant, 40 hours on flashing

USB-C

Abus may be better known for its D-locks and chains, but the German brand also has a nice line in helmets.

Founded in 1924 by August Bremicker, Abus has gradually built a helmet range that runs from race lids to kids' helmets, with a particularly strong urban line.

The Hyp-E is the brand's flagship e-bike helmet line, and it scooped a Eurobike Award in 2024. Where Abus' more basic Pedelec 2.0 helmet relies on a pull-out rain cap to fend off the elements, the Hyp-E goes one better with in-built sliding vent covers. It also goes all-in on visibility too, with integrated front and rear lights that act as indicators, triggered by a wireless remote on your handlebar.

Like its Pedelec stablemate, the Hyp-E carries Dutch NTA 8776 certification, which means it's been tested at the higher impact speeds you can reach with a motor under you, and it covers more of the head than a standard bike helmet.

The Hyp-E comes in three versions that all essentially use the same base helmet but come with increasingly flashy add-ons. The standard model reviewed here includes integrated lights, an indicator remote and a vent cover for when the weather turns. The ACE adds a magnetic flip-up visor and clip-on ear pads, and the BL.ACE adds a brake light remote on top of that. Those extras can also be bought separately, so the standard Hyp-E is effectively the base you can build up from.

I tested the standard Hyp-E on both electrically-assisted rides around town, as well as on my 40-minute, pedal-powered commute. Being early autumn, I enjoyed some warmer rides but was also faced with some biblical downpours, so the helmet got properly put to the test.

By design, the e-bike helmet is a bigger piece of kit than the everyday commuter helmet. The NTA 8776 certificate dictates that the shell needs to cover a larger proportion of the head. Add to that some integrated lights and vent covers and the size and weight is only going one way.

While the Hyp-E isn’t the bulkiest design on the market, it’s not exactly petite either. It’s not as streamlined as the Pedelec 2.0, but it’s not as big as some of the other smart helmet options, such as the Unit 1 Aura .

Abus calls the construction a multishell design, as part of the outer surface uses a tougher hard shell while the rest is a thinner in-mould polycarbonate layer. A polycarbonate strip also wraps the lower edge to protect against scuffs, which is welcomed by the tester as it will inevitably end up being knocked about a bit.

The lights are undeniably the stars of the show. Rather than clipping on as an afterthought, the front and rear LED strips are moulded into the shell, sitting flush with the contours. With the lights switched off, the helmet looks clean and tidy. With them on, you're highly visible.

The outer shell comes down lower at the temples and the back of the head than a standard helmet, as required by the NTA 8776 standard. Up top, the vents are generous by urban helmet standards, and the Hyp-E comes with a vent cover that slides over them when the weather turns.

Out of the box, the standard Hyp-E is the most stripped-back version of the three helmets in this range. There's no visor or ear pads to bulk it out, just the shell, the lights and a set of MagneticHub mounting points at the front. Those points are there so you can add Abus's magnetic visor, in clear, smoke or photochromic, and the clip-on Ear Pads (also sold separately). Add both and the Hyp-E takes on a distinctly motorcycle-like look, which personally feels a bit much, especially if you plan on using it on pedal-powered rides.

The standard Hyp-E also has the widest choice of colours in the range, giving you a choice between evocative names such as Champagne Gold, Jungle Green and Volcano Titan. The Midnight Blue that I tested had a nice matte finish across the shell, with a grey rear section housing the rear light, with some subtle touches of exposed EPS.

As soon as you pick up the Hyp-E, you’ll notice how robust it feels. Abus combines both in-mould and hard-shell production methods, which is why the helmet appears to have two distinct sections. The in-mould process fuses the EPS liner into a thin polycarbonate outer during production, while the hard-shell process involves manufacturing the liner and outer shell separately and then sticking them together. The in-mould process gives the Hyp-E its protective lower edge and rear section, while the hard shell allows for the slidable vents.

Safety is underpinned by NTA 8776, the Dutch e-bike standard that requires testing at higher impact speeds and extra coverage around the temples and back of the head. The helmet also carries CE and US CPSC certification. What it doesn't have is MIPS or any other rotational impact system, which is a notable omission at this price, and there's no Virginia Tech rating to back up the protection claims either.

The headline feature, of course, is the lighting. Rather than offering clip-on units, the front and rear LEDs are integrated into the shell, come with six modes – steady, power, flow, pulse, flash and eco – and boast an output of up to 50 lumens. Runtime ranges from a claimed minimum of two hours on the brightest steady setting to 40 hours in flashing mode, and the lithium-polymer battery takes around four hours to charge via USB-C. That's a welcome step up from the Micro-USB port and 10 lumens on the Abus Pedelec 2.0.

As well as providing a good source of visibility, the lights double as indicators, and the helmet comes with a wireless remote that straps to your handlebar. Pressing either button triggers a sequential sweep on the relevant side of the helmet, front and rear. Press both at once and you get a hazard-warning function. The remote is simple and connects via a radio link system, rather than Bluetooth, so there's no app to set up.

The standard Hyp-E doesn't include the brake light remote, which comes with the top-tier BL.ACE. Rather than relying on an accelerometer to guess when you're slowing down, Abus's brake light uses a rubberised cap that slips over your brake lever and fires when you pull it. It can be bought separately if you want to add it later.

Fit is handled by the Zoom Spin dial system, which uses a full headring and is height-adjustable, with an opening to accommodate ponytails. Abus's strap dividers lock in place below the ears, and they fasten with a magnetic buckle that can be opened one-handed.

Ventilation comes from three closable intakes on top of the helmet and two exhausts at the rear. The intakes are backed by bug mesh, and the included Vent Cover clips over them to block out rain, wind and cold. If you find you want more weather protection, the Hyp-E can be upgraded with the visor and ear pads that come with the Hyp-E ACE.

Even without those extras, the Hyp-E is no featherweight. At a claimed 580g for a medium, it weighs considerably more than the 350g Pedelec 2.0 and sits at the heavier end of the e-bike helmet category. That's the price you pay for high-quality integrated lights and battery.

I’ve been testing a lot of different e-bike helmets over the last six months, and picking my favourites for the best e-bike helmets has been a tough task. While the Hyp-E didn’t quite make the cut, it still performed extremely well in a range of conditions.

My top two criteria when researching helmets are safety and comfort. While I’m not paid nearly enough to put the Hyp-E’s safety credentials fully to the test, you can rest assured that some thorough testing has been carried out by people far more qualified than me. The NTA 8776 certificate is the gold standard when it comes to e-bike lids, and I would hesitate in recommending a helmet without it.

When it comes to comfort, there is of course an element of subjectivity, and to go some way to mitigating that, I did pass my Abus round a few friends for a second opinion. The consensus is that it is a pretty comfy piece of kit.

The Hyp-E uses a full 360-degree headring within the cradle, which means that any pressure that comes from tightening the dial adjust should be spread out, rather than being applied from the front or back, which can be the case with 180-degree rings. The fact that the rear section and dial adjust can be moved up and down only adds to the level of customisation when it comes to fit. It also allows for ponytails.

The strap doesn’t boast the reflective thread like the Pedelec 2.0, but otherwise it’s got some nice touches. The magnetic buckle is an advancement in fastening that I am fully on board with. Being able to unbuckle one-handed when you come crashing through the door after a wet and windy commute is the kind of small win I am here for. In addition, the soft chin guard beneath the buckle is held in place by Velcro, which saves you having to line it up every time you do the thing up.

For me, the two big plus points on the Hyp-E are the retractable vents and the integrated lights. Abus have clearly set out to make a line of e-bike helmets for all seasons and conditions. By including three big front vents, it has done what so many modern e-bike helmet manufacturers have failed to do, and allow sufficient airflow for warmer days. But by adding the slide-down covers, the design accounts for wet, cold and windy days, too. Abus has done this on the Pedelec 2.0 as well, although the cover comes in the shape of a tiny anorak which packs into a compartment at the rear of the shell.

In testing, the vents did exactly what they were designed to do, letting a decent amount of air in at the front and out through the rear. The vent covers are easy to close while riding, with a single slider fitted at the top of the shell.

Having tested this during early autumn, I was faced with a decision on those wet-but-still-warm rides. With the vents closed, the airflow is completely shut down, so it does get a bit warm. Honourable mention here to the Lazer Verde which has tried (with limited success) to create vents that both let air in but keep rain out. The Pedelec’s anorak should probably get another mention here, as that does at least allow some breathability.

With the nights starting to draw in, I was really glad to have the option of extremely effective integrated front and rear lights. At 50 lumens these aren’t the brightest (honourable nod to the Unit 1 Aura), but when it gets properly dark they really stand out. In addition, they wrap a long way round the shell, giving you a better chance of being seen by vehicles approaching from the side.

Once you get to know the button and the modes, it’s easy enough to operate whilst riding, and the USB-C charger means you’re not forever hunting through drawers for an old lead.

I’m a big fan of these lights, and while I’d always recommend pairing them with some decent bike lights as well, the extra visibility goes a long way. As far as the indicators go, I’m not fully convinced turn signals via a helmet light is something drivers are fully tuned into, but that will inevitably change if and when the technology becomes more widely used.

The indicators on the Hyp-E go produce a very clear flashing light on the right or left of the helmet, and the colour switches from red to yellow. This means anyone paying attention will see a pretty distinct signal, as opposed to mistaking it for just another mode. The handlebar-mounted switch was easily paired with the helmet in a matter of seconds, and also charges via USB-C.

I didn’t get a chance to fully put Abus’ claims around helmet battery life to the test, but the lowest output mode (which I assume gets you the maximum 40 hours of charge) is frankly pretty crap compared to the other settings. So I would assume the time between charges to be considerably shorter than that.…

title: Canyon Grail CF SLX review: More capable than ever before, but perhaps not quite as fun
author: thomas.wieckowski@futurenet.com (Tom Wieckowski)
text:
$5,499 / £4,799 / €4,999

9kg (S) out of the box with sealant, computer mount, cages, storage bag and tools.

SRAM Force XPLR - 10-46T / 40T

Strawberry Shake / Metallic Acid / Monochrome

The Grail has been in the Canyon range since 2018 and is the brand's racier, performance-oriented model.

Gravel bikes designed for competition are becoming more aerodynamic, race-focused, and are getting bigger clearances; this latest update sees Canyon take the Grail down that path further still.

The new machine is more aero, lower, racier and now has 57mm tyre clearance. The previous Grail had 42mm clearance, so this is a big jump. That smaller clearance number was probably the key weak spot in the 2nd-gen bikes' armour as gravel machines progressed at pace.

Canyon said it took its time with this update, and wanted to keep the Grail feeling like a Grail. I can understand that; the previous bike was one of the best gravel bikes and was pretty much universally regarded as a strong all-rounder.

This time around, I have tested the CF SLX 8 AXS, the model I also tested last time, in the eye-catching 'Strawberry Shake' colourway. The price for this second-tier CF SLX model is $5,999 / £4,799 / €4,999.

You can see the outgoing Grail up above and compare the visual differences, but let's cover what exactly has changed first.

Tyre clearance has really been boosted from 42mm up to 57mm, and that new number is a big talking point when it comes to the new Grail.

Canyon has achieved this by using a thin but solid section of driveside chainstay and by growing the rear chainstays by 10mm. Up front, a revised fork provides plenty of clearance. 57mm + 4mm either side in line with ISO guidelines.

The new frame is a little heavier; my Gen 2 CF SLX 8 weighed in at 8.2 kg out of the box. This time we were at 9kg on my scales. If you're a racer, the increased aero will probably make you faster, depending on speed, but as a general gravel bike for an everyday rider, I think the added weight at times makes the bike feel just a touch less nimble.

The frame has some deeper tube profiles and more aero overall shapes; you can read about Canyon's claims regarding aero performance in our Grail news piece .

On the aero topic, there's also a new, more aerodynamic seatpost, the SP0093 VCLS. Canyon says it offers 25% more vertical compliance than a rigid unit.

The front end is more aggressive; it's now 15mm lower, but Canyon is speccing shorter stems on models. Small to large bikes come with an 80mm stem as well as an adjustable 390-440cm bar. The stem has been pretty much ideal for me, but bigger riders or those wanting a long reach may want or need a longer front end.

On the geometry, the Grail has received some slight tweaks, but on paper things are very similar to the old bike. For a small, my size, the head tube angle of 71.5 degrees stays the same, and the seat tube angle steepens slightly, going from 73.5 to 73.9 degrees.

The chainstays have grown by 10mm, and the wheelbase is 5mm longer. The stack is 15mm lower, whilst the reach number is the same.

That stem is part of the adjustable CP0048 integrated handlebar with width-adjustable Control bar drops. You can buy alternate drops or handlebars, but you will have to pay extra to do it.

The CF SLX model also has full fender mounts, something the race-focused CFR model doesn't. If you choose to use the Canyon FAST Fender system, you won't be disappointed; it's very easy to use and provides excellent protection in bad weather. Don't forget you may need to come down in tyre size with them depending on what you are running.

Canyon has also produced some new frame storage bags for the bike in partnership with Cyclite; these are lightweight options and integrate neatly. They are available separately for $119.99 for the big bag, and $69.99 for the top tube option.

The CF SLX 8 arrived with a solid range of equipment. There's an excellent SRAM Force XPLR groupset with a left-hand power meter. Stock cranks are also 165mm in length, very on-trend.

The wheels are carbon fibre DT Swiss GRC 1400s, a hardy and aerodynamic option. They are wrapped in 45mm Schwalbe G One RS tyres. Some may criticise the decision not to fit a 50mm+ tyre from the off, but there is nothing wrong with the stock 45mm tyres.

I'm constantly impressed by just how capable a good gravel bike is these days. They can do so much, so well. The Grail CF SLX is no exception; it's performed well everywhere.

It goes fast on the flat and on smoother gravel and broken tarmac. I often leave the road behind on my to-go loop and enter a short descent into a long, straight gravel track; I get the Grail up to speed there, and it just eats the road up.

That lower front end helps a touch, but the bike doesn't feel aggressively low; it's a measured change. I like it.

The bike is stable at speed and under hard braking in the drops, and handles rough technical sections well. There's no doubt this is a hugely capable bike; I haven't found it wanting in any one area. The bar has been raised wholesale with modern gravel bikes; the differences are finer and more specific now, I find.

The Grail is undoubtedly more race-oriented; however, I don't find the CF SLX super stiff, and it doesn't feel quite as agile and, dare I say it, as fast as the Argon 18 Anti Matter I rode in the summer did.

It's a calmer experience with the Grail; it has not put a foot wrong on any terrain during my testing, but at times the ride feels a little muted.

Perhaps it's the capability of the overall package that just makes things feel calmer, or the longer chainstays, bigger rubber and slightly heavier wheelset (1600+ grams) on this model reducing some playfulness.

I started on the stock Schwalbe G One R 45mm tyres, then switched to big 2.2" Continental Dubnital tyres in their fastest version, and went back to the 45s, and I think I had more fun on the 45s at home riding solo.

The big tyres fit comfortably, and part of the reason for switching was to verify the bike's clearance myself. It's there, and the bike's proportions still look very normal. Canyon has executed it very well.

It's heartening to know that big clearance is there for when you need it, but a 45 or a 50mm tyre is still very capable, and the bike feels a little more nimble and exciting to ride, in my opinion. I'd maybe go big where needed if I was racing a gravel calendar, and run a 45 or 50mm tyre at home.

My standard advice now is to shop for a gravel bike with a SRAM XPLR 1x groupset if you are looking for a gravel bike. They are fantastic groupsets for off-road riding. I have no complaints about the drivetrain performance, and the brakes are fantastic for scrubbing off speed off-road.

At times my knees have scuffed the Cyclite top tube bag; I've found the bag material quite rough, sharp on the edges, even. It's my problem, but long term I'd probably need a different bag, or even no bag, to prevent knee grazing.

The strong speccing continues through the CF SLX 8 model; the drivetrain is excellent, and the wheel and tyres package is great; the Schwalbe G-One tyres are excellent all-rounders. The wheelset is a touch on the heavier side in its 50mm version; perhaps some lighter wheels may help boost the feeling of acceleration and nimbleness.

Aside from some rough bag material, the Grail has performed perfectly. No mechanical issues of any kind, which is always good.

Maintenance and servicing

We're heading into winter here in the UK, and my thoughts are already turning to winter maintenance. I've had to hose down a muddy Grail a few times already.

At risk of sounding like a broken record, the key maintenance area to watch here is the integrated handlebar and stem assembly. You can't remove the stem easily, so trapped water and dirt will stay inside the headset/head tube area. A full strip-down for replacements will be expensive. Look after it by minimising aggressive hosing, and consider a front fender in some conditions.

Elsewhere, I'd recommend staying on top of the seatpost clamp assembly, thru-axles, and AXS rear derailleur sleeve in general. There's also a press-fit bottom bracket, which shouldn't cause too much of a headache, really. Though, of course, creaks do arise sometimes.

You're starting in a competitive place immediately with Canyon's direct pricing.

This bike costs $5,999 / £4,799 / €4,999 at RRP. The SRAM Force XPLR-equipped Factor Sarana I tested in the summer costs $2,500 more than this bike. Though you can spec your desired bar width and stem length at checkout with the Factor.

There's a solid spec with no gaps here, and any and all spare parts or hardware you might need are easily found on the Canyon site. The Grail range also has several cheaper bikes with this, and in my experience, Canyon bike specs are generally solid.

As ever with Canyon models, it would be nice to get the computer mount included with the bike, and you will, of course, need to buy any accesories you need separately, such as the frame storage bag, frame bags, or mudguards.

The latest Canyon Grail is a massively capable bike that will handle pretty much whatever you throw at it; it's a tank.

Canyon has given it a thorough update and improved the areas that were seen as the weaknesses of the old bike, namely the conservative tyre clearance. Riders and racers alike can now go as large as they want depending on preference or the demands of a course, that's to say nothing of mud clearance.

As I said in my first ride piece, the Grail still largely feels like a Grail; performance and capability have increased. I'll hammer the point home: this is a massively capable gravel bike, but it isn't quite as lively as the previous bike.

Perhaps this is where gravel bikes are now heading; if you're a racer looking for the most capable aero race bike with big clearance, you can just get on and race, then step this way.

Very nice, I think the frame looks very 'normal' for the big 57mm clearance, and the frame looks agressive and purposeful. I like the 'Strawberry shake' paint too.

Very solid, excellent groupset, solid wheels and tyres and Canyon's equipment works wekk. The wheels are a little on the heavier side, and may not help acceleration.

Super capable and fast in any terrain. Clearance provides more tyre choice than ever before. The ride feel does feel a little muted at times. I don't feel the seatpost adds much in the way of comfort.

9kg for a small out of the box without pedals, and with accesories. Not superlight, in line with other competitor models.

Very good, a solid spec and overall build. As ever with Canyon, it would be nice to get the computer inluded.

title: Carrick arrives at training ground with future unclear
text:
Eddie Howe and Julian Nagelsmann are emerging as early contenders to become the next Manchester United head coach if Michael Carrick loses his job.

Carrick's position at Old Trafford is under major threat following the club's poor start to the season, with work towards identifying his successor believed to be ongoing.

It is understood Howe and Nagelsmann both feature prominently on the list of candidates the club has explored to potentially replace him, and that both managers are aware of United's interest.

Sources have also indicated Aston Villa boss Unai Emery is admired at United, but the fact he is under contract would complicate any move for the Spaniard.

Howe, Nagelsmann and Antonio Conte – who is interested in the job – are out of work, making their potential appointments easier.

Multiple sources have told BBC Sport that former Newcastle boss Howe is fully open to joining United if Carrick loses his job.

Nagelsmann is available after leaving his job as Germany head coach after the World Cup, while Conte – who has also been linked with Juventus – is open to returning to football after leaving Napoli in May.

Should Carrick be dismissed, the 20-time English top-flight champions will be looking to appoint their eighth permanent manager or head coach since Sir Alex Ferguson departed the club in 2013 on the back of winning their most recent title.

Here, BBC Sport takes a closer look at the contenders who could be up for the job.

The Englishman has been out of work since leaving Newcastle in the summer.

Howe, 48, helped the Magpies end their 56-year wait for a trophy when he led them to League Cup glory in 2025 and secured two Champions League qualifications in his five years in charge.

The former Bournemouth and Burnley boss is available and would be considered. Sources have indicated Howe is open to returning to management with United specifically after leaving St James' Park in the close season.

The Italian has been out of work since leaving Napoli in June and is interested in the job.

Conte has won Serie A titles with three different clubs as manager - Juventus, Inter Milan and Napoli.

The 57-year-old led Chelsea to the Premier League title in 2017 and FA Cup in 2018. During his time at Tottenham between November 2021 and March 2023 he helped them qualify for the Champions League.

Also out of work, interested and high up on the club's list of contenders.

The German left the role of manager of his country's national team after a World Cup last-32 defeat on penalties to Paraguay last summer, having lost in the quarter-finals of Euro 2024 to Spain.

Nagelsmann, 39, earned his reputation as a young coach at Hoffenheim and RB Leipzig before he landed the Bayern Munich job in 2021. He led them to the Bundesliga title in 2022 but was sacked the following season amid fluctuating form.

The Aston Villa head coach's stock is high at United given how he has steered the Midlands club to Champions League qualification twice since arriving in 2022.

However, he would be difficult to prise from his current role given his contract runs until 2029.

Emery, 54, has won five Europa League trophies at Sevilla, Villarreal and at his current club while he also helped Paris St-Germain to domestic honours in a two-year stint there.

However, he lasted just 18 months at Arsenal before being sacked in 2019.

The Brighton manager is another who is well liked at Old Trafford, but the Seagulls would have little interest in discussing his availability.

It would be a difficult deal to do financially for Man Utd as well.

Hurzeler, 33, guided German club St Pauli to promotion to the Bundesliga in 2024 before he was picked up by Brighton where he is enjoying a very strong start to his third season at the club.

The former Arsenal midfielder masterminded United's humiliating 4-1 defeat in Como on Wednesday night in a game that pushed Carrick to the brink.

Fabregas, 39, is considered one of the best young coaches in Europe for his work in helping to steer the Italian club from Serie B to the Champions League and will be wanted by many major clubs in the coming months.

title: 'Still so much I want to achieve' – Jay Vine commits future to UAE Team Emirates-XRG with 2029 contract extension
author: Owen Rogers
text:
After a season blighted by poor luck and injury, Jay Vine has committed his long-term future to UAE Team Emirates-XRG, extending his contract until the end of the 2029 season.

This will bring the Australian time trial champion's time on the Emirati team to a total of seven seasons, having joined in 2023. Since then, he has developed into an elite time trialist, breakaway hunter, and fine domestique, contributing to others’ successes while still able to take his own opportunities.

Vine, 30, began his time at UAE with overall victory at the Tour Down Under, bagging the first of two general classification successes in his home race. He followed that with stage wins at the Vuelta a España, where he has twice won the mountains classification, the Tour de Romandie, Coppi e Bartali and the Vuelta a Burgos.

Despite beginning his 2026 season by winning a stage and second GC title at the Tour Down Under, his 2026 has been far from plain sailing. On stage five of that very race, he was hit by a kangaroo which jumped into the peloton , sustaining a broken bone in his wrist, though was still able to finish and take the GC.

Returning for the Volta a Ciclista a Catalunya, he crashed out on stage three, before being one of two UAE riders forced to abandon the Giro d’Italia after a huge crash on wet roads during stage 2 , this time leaving him with a fractured elbow and concussion.

There was more bad fortune at the Vuelta a Burgos, where he again crashed out, before illness forced him out of the Vuelta a España. However, he bounced back to close his season with second place at the Chrono des Nations , behind a rampant Remco Evenepoel (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe).

"I’m really happy to be continuing with the team until 2029," Vine said in a team statement. "I couldn’t imagine a better fit, and I’m incredibly grateful for the trust and support I’ve been shown here, both in the good times and the more difficult ones. That support means a lot to me and is something I really value about this team.

"I’m already building towards the 2027 season and can’t wait to get started. There’s still so much I want to achieve, and I’m excited to keep working alongside some genuine friends, and see what we can accomplish together over the coming years."

title: After three-decade gap, Basque company Etxeondo joins forces again with Movistar as apparel sponsor
author: Alasdair Fotheringham
text:
Movistar have confirmed that Basque company Etxeondo will once again be their apparel sponsor from 2027 onwards, reviving a collaboration that lasted through much of the historic Spanish team's 'golden age' of the 1980s and early 1990s.

Etxeondo last sponsored Movistar back when it was the Reynolds squad, beginning in 1983 through to the mid 1990s, by which time the team's main backer was the Spanish bank, Banesto.

During that time, Reynolds/Banesto became a pioneering force for Spanish cycling in the Giro d'Italia and Tour de France as the country bounced back from its lacklustre era of the late 1970s. The team won the Tour with Pedro Delgado in 1988 and then Miguel Indurain f rom 1991 through to 1995, with Indurain also claiming the country's first-ever victories in the Giro in 1992 and 1993.

The return of Etxeondo as clothing sponsor for Movistar covers both the men's and women's teams, although the actual design of the new kit for both squads will likely only be revealed in early 2027.

"We are renewing a relationship that goes all the way back to the Reynolds years," Movistar said in a team press release. "It's a new phase which unites history with the development of race-competition apparel."

"Aerodynamics, comfort and protection in different kinds of weather will be the main focus points of our collaboration."

"The knowledge gained will have benefits beyond professional cycling. Etxeondo will transfer what is learned in the team to the development of its products to improve the experience of those who enjoy cycling every day."

Founded in the Basque Country in 1976, Etxeondo has spent the last five decades dedicated to the design and development of cycling clothing. It currently has two bases, in the towns of Irura (Gipuzkoa) and Castejón (Navarre).
