title: $85 Million Cost and $130 Tickets: The 2027 Tour de France Grand Départ is Blowing the Budget
author: Jim Cotton
text:
The grands départs of the 2027 men’s and women’s Tour de France are being slated as the most expensive bike races ever held.

British journalist Jeremy Whittle reported last week that the UK government will invest a total of £65m GBP (~$85m USD) into hosting the grands départs of next year’s Tour de France and Tour de France Femmes .

Spanning six days of racing across Scotland, Wales, and England, each stage will cost a staggering equivalent of £11m (~$15m).

And that’s not the only wild expense associated with the Tour’s British start.

The opening ceremony and team presentation of the men’s race will be fully ticketed, with the most premium seats being sold for £99 a pop. That’s just north of $130 for the privilege of seeing Tadej Pogačar and his comrades doing some bemused waving on a big stage.

For race organizer ASO, an overseas start is a lucrative money spinner. It charges host nations millions of Euros for the honor. In return, hosts can use the Tour de France as a promotional platform and legacy investment.

However, next year’s grands départs – the men’s 28th overseas jaunt and the women’s third – will be extraordinary business.

Whittle reported eye-watering expenses associated with the privilege of being the first nation to host a partnered men’s and women’s event.

Running out of Edinburgh on July 2 for the men’s race and from Leeds on July 30 for the Femmes, Whittle called the six stages of the $85m USD carnival “the most expensive bike races ever held.”

For context, the 2014 UK grand départ reportedly cost the British government £29.4m.

While it’s comparing apples to oranges, the full cost of the 11-day multi-format Glasgow “super worlds” in 2023 nudged toward £63m.

But how can a few hundred kilometers of the Tour de France be so costly?

The hosting fees paid over to the race organizer are huge, and they’re only the start.

ASO is thought to have charged around €10m euros (~£8m or $11m) for the rights to host recent grands départ s in Florence (2024) and Barcelona (2026). The hosting charges for 2027 are unknown.

After that, costs associated with staging the biggest bike races in the world include security, road resurfacing, preparing local infrastructure, and supporting all the random side-events that pop up when the Tour comes to town.

The UK Government has projected economic benefits of more than £150m from the combined 2027 men’s and women’s race.

One particular side-event of the 2027 Tour de France has garnered particular interest – and stirred significant controversy – in recent weeks.

The opening ceremony and team presentation of the men’s Tour on Wednesday 30 June will be fully ticketed, and admission ain’t cheap.

Tickets for the event on the esplanade outside Edinburgh Castle span from £27 ($36) for “bring the binoculars” seats high in the stands to £99 ($130) for primo spots.

Pogačar and the peloton will trundle on and off the stage as part of a mash-up ceremony that includes a show by The Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo. The traditional Scottish event is a bagpipes ‘n’ kilts show including music, dance, and rock concert lighting.

Details of the Tour de France Femmes opening ceremony have not yet been confirmed.

It’s rare, but not unprecedented, for Tour de France team presentations to be ticketed.

However, the past three, held in suitably spectacular settings in Barcelona, Lille, and Florence, were all free to attend.

News that next year’s team presentation will be ticketed has, of course, stirred debate.

The Tour de France does sell itself on being “the biggest free sporting event in the world,” after all.

When Whittle enquired about the charges as part of his Substack report, a representative argued for the event’s extraordinary nature.

“This isn’t a standard team presentation,” a Grand Départ GB told Whittle. “By partnering with The Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo, we’re creating a one-off event that fans won’t have seen before at a grand départ, and ticketing reflects that.

“As with any team presentation, the riders will take a route through the city before arriving at Edinburgh Castle, in this case from Holyrood Palace via the Royal Mile to the castle, which will be completely unticketed,” they added.

The representative also reminded Whittle every kilometer of all three stages of the men’s grand départ will be open access.

“The race itself stays free,” they said. “Spectators will have free access to more than 900km of roadside across both grands départs, and we expect people to come out in their millions to cheer on the world’s best male and female riders.”

If the ticket fees aren’t steep enough to put you off the prospect of some traditional Scottish dance and some bemused pro cyclists, tickets go on general sale here on October 30.

title: Mads Pedersen among group of Danish athletes suing HBO over use of their images for advertising
author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
text:
Mads Pedersen is among a group of Danish athletes suing streaming service HBO Max over unauthorised use of their images.

Cyclists Amalie Dideriksen, Mikkel Bjerg , and Sebastian Fini Carstensen are also part of the lawsuit, which encompasses 13 athletes requesting 2 million Danish Kroner (DKK) – around £224,000 – in compensation.

In the lawsuit, the group of athletes, including athletes from other sports, are claiming 50,000 DKK (£5,600) per image HBO Nordic used in the run-up to the Paris Olympic Games in 2024.

Pedersen appeared in court via video link on Monday.

"It's difficult to sell my name and image to others if it's used for free," he said, according to .

"I believe without a doubt that it was for the purpose of selling a product. It has been harmful to the extent that I try to sell my picture and image to others.

"There are other companies that pay large sums of money for that. And I did not give HBO permission to use those photos."

Pedersen pointed to several of his own brand advertising deals. He noted that workwear brand Airtox is paying him 3.4 million DKK (£380,000) for a two-year deal to use his image, while Lidl-Trek's clothing sponsor Crivit is paying him 19 million DKK (£2.1 million) over five years.

Lawyers representing the group claim images of the athletes were used on HBO Max's website, Facebook and Instagram accounts and on a large banner advert in Copenhagen,

HBO's counterclaim is that its use of images should be considered in an editorial context, according to TV2.

Pedersen is claiming 150,000 DKK (£16,800) in compensation for three uses of his image. Other athletes in the lawsuit, badminton player Victor Axelsen and handball player Mathias Gidsel, have larger compensation claims of 450,000 DKK (£50,000).

What Marco Rubio’s sidestepping of New Delhi says about the US’s stance on India
author: Niha Masih
text:
Rubio’s decision not to meet Narendra Modi last week was seen by some as a snub – but by focusing on business leaders and oil, the secretary of state made American priorities clear. Plus: the artist bringing a female perspective to men’s clothing

Don’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

When the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio , visited India for the second time this year, headlines concentrated on who he met and where he went.

The fact that Rubio bypassed New Delhi and did not meet the prime minister, Narendra Modi, during his trip last week, and instead traveled to the financial capital, Mumbai, where he met India’s foreign minister, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar (pictured top with Rubio), and business leaders, did not go unnoticed. Nor did his decision to travel to Jamnagar, the small Gujarati town that is home to Reliance Industries’ colossal oil refinery complex.

Bilateral ties between the two countries have come under strain under the second Trump administration, particularly over tariffs and India’s purchase of Russian oil. Yet, Rubio’s return to India just five months after his first visit as secretary of state signals that the country remains useful for president Donald Trump’s ambitions after all.

As director of the South Asia Program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, Milan Vaishnav has spent a decade tracking India’s place in the world, particularly its ties with the US. Vaishnav has described Trump 2.0 as “unbound” marking a new era in India-US relations.

Tracking foreign affairs, he told me, is a minefield right now. From the White House’s transactional approach to global alliances, ongoing conflicts in the Middle East and consequential elections around the world, politics is changing at a pace that means all predictions are off the table. “I think anyone who tells you they know exactly what is going on and how it fits into their neat theory of the world is lying to you,” says Vaishnav.

I asked him about the many confusing aspects of the US-India relationship, from the hostile political rhetoric to the US embrace of Pakistan, as well as Rubio’s latest visit.

Ahead of Rubio’s visit, several commentators noted the secretary of state’s “unusual” itinerary . Vaishnav thought the pre-visit chatter about Rubio skipping Delhi to visit Mumbai and Jamnagar was overblown. “Not every bilateral meeting has to take place in a national capital,” he says.

But that doesn’t mean it wasn’t noteworthy. “I do think the choice of venues was intentional. This administration and, particularly, this president, sees foreign policy through the lens of ‘deal-making’. And if you’re trying to drum up business deals, what better place to visit than Mumbai?” he says.

The Jamnagar visit, where Rubio met Mukesh Ambani, the chair of Reliance, also indicates some politicking. “At a time when petrol prices are extremely high in the United States and are likely to be a major issue in the 3 November midterm elections, the administration wants to show that it is doing everything it can to bring them down. India is a major consumer of oil, but it is also a major exporter of refined petroleum products,” says Vaishnav. “One of Rubio’s objectives was to encourage Reliance and, by extension, India to process more Venezuelan crude [oil],” he added.

While this could present an opportunity for India to advance relations, it’s not a given: the US president remains, after all – and to put it lightly – mercurial.

“The biggest plot twist for me has been the Trump administration’s embrace of Pakistan after the May 2025 conflict with India,” says Vaishnav. Pakistan’s standing in Washington had eroded over the years, especially under Joe Biden, who left office without ever having made a presidential phone call to his counterpart in Pakistan. “Many officials in Congress had grown exhausted with Pakistan’s double game, speaking the language of partnership on the one hand while undermining US interests on the other,” says Vaishnav.

But, after coming to power the second time, Trump thanked the country for its help in nabbing a suspect linked to a 2021 bombing in Afghanistan that killed 13 US service members. This reversal in Pakistan’s fortunes gathered pace after the May conflict with India, which Trump took credit for ending. In June, he welcomed Asim Munir , Pakistan’s army chief, to the White House, after Munir called for the president to be nominated for the Nobel peace prize.

“I chalk up the reversal to a few factors: Trump’s well-known strongman envy, Pakistan’s savvy diplomacy, and the prospect of energy and crypto deals involving members of Trump’s inner circle,” says Vaishnav. For him, it isyet another demonstration of how much weight Trump places on deals, transactions and short-term wins. “For New Delhi, this means Modi’s personal rapport with Trump and 25 years of investment in the bilateral relationship offer no guarantee against a 180-degree reversal in US policy,” he adds.

In a recent piece , Vaishnav’s colleague Sameer Lalwani pointed out that the US relationship with India remains more resilient than the political rhetoric may suggest with quiet, but nonetheless strategic, progress being made.

As Lalwani points out, bilateral trade reached a record high between India and the US in 2025; nearly $68bn worth of AI infrastructure investment in India has been pledged by US technology companies; and the two countries have carried out record number of joint military exercises this year.…

title: How much of Antonelli's success is down to his ability? - F1 Q&A
text:
Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli is one step closer to becoming the new F1 world champion after winning the United States Grand Prix from pole position.

The 20-year-old Italian, who leads team-mate George Russell by 123 points in the standings, will secure the title in Mexico City on Sunday by finishing ninth or higher.

BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions after the race in Austin.

Antonelli delivers 'the race of a champion who isn't the champion yet'

This weekend, both Mercedes drivers had the new upgrades but Kimi Antonelli dominated qualifying and the race while George Russell didn't quite achieve the same success. There is a theme throughout the season. How much of that is down to driver ability, driving style etc and how much is down to car set-up and strategy. Is George better than this or has he reached his limit? - Julian

The dominant theme of the 2026 season has been the degree to which Kimi Antonelli has stepped up his game after a mixed rookie season that contained some definite highs, but also quite a few difficulties.

In doing so, he has overwhelmed George Russell, who has accepted and is more than willing to say that Antonelli has simply done a better job than him this season.

Antonelli's performances this year have lived up to the billing with which he came to F1 - that he could be the sport's next generational talent.

He has had some luck, and some of his wins have turned on fortune - safety cars in Japan and Madrid, for example.

But he has also performed at a level of consistent excellence, and produced some absolutely standout performances, most obviously Monaco, Monza and Austin.

The Mercedes has on average been the best car, but Antonelli is the only one of the team's two drivers who has always been a factor. He fully deserves the world title that he is almost certain to clinch this weekend in Mexico City.

As for Russell, he has fundamentally used driving style as an explanation for his relative struggles, saying the previous cars suited his, and the new ones Antonelli's. He has won only three races compared with Antonelli's nine.

On Sunday, team principal Toto Wolff said Russell had struggled in Austin to get the right set-up on the Mercedes with the new upgrade package, which has been problematic since it was introduced in Malaysia.

Wolff said: "George, for all of us in the team, is a champion and has won in every category and merits to be put in the group of the very best ones. And we've seen that last year.

"This year, we see this variability in results. When we land the car in the way that suits him, he's absolutely fine. But when it drops out of that operational window, he struggles and he struggles more than maybe Kimi. And that is on us.

"We just have to work it out with him how there can be such a difference in driving, in performance, because George is not half a second slower, three tenths slower than Kimi. That's just absolutely not the case.

"So what is it that he doesn't like? What is it that we need to do in terms of modifying the car, setting it up in a different way for him to go fast? Because it's all about the intelligence, the ability, the determination."

Driving style and set-up are genuine reasons for a driver to struggle in certain circumstances.

However, it's also a case that the absolute elite, the all-time greats - drivers such as Max Verstappen, Lewis Hamilton and Fernando Alonso - tend to find a way to be at the top of their game regardless of the car's behaviour.

The worry for Russell right now is that if Antonelli is at that level - and it looks as though he has the potential to be, given his performances in only his second season - he will have his work cut out to beat him consistently in the future.

So he needs to regroup over the winter, come back next year and prove he can get back on to Antonelli's level.

With Lewis Hamilton's intentions clear of staying in F1 until there is an African Grand Prix, which I think will most likely be with Ferrari, what does that mean for the young talents who desire to drive for Ferrari? Will it be at least another four to five years before we see new drivers replacing either or both Lewis and Charles Leclerc? - Liam

Lewis Hamilton repeated in Austin last weekend that, ideally, he would like to still be racing when Formula 1 returns to Africa.

"I'm now forced to have to stay a lot longer because we have a race in Africa and that's been my dream, to be able to race in Africa," he said.

"So, yes, I have to keep fighting to try and stay fit. If I can still punch out good results over the next year, we'll keep it going."

Whether he can manage to stay that long is another question.

Formula 1 has said the African Grand Prix in Rwanda will be held in the "early 2030s".

The aim is for that to be in 2030 but it's not clear whether the new track will be ready by then.

Even if they make that deadline, will Hamilton still be racing? He will be 45 at the start of 2030. That's the same age as Fernando Alonso is now, and he is still going strong.

Hamilton's answer alludes to his current contract, which it is believed lasts until the end of 2027. So he would need to do another one of three years to make it to 2030.

As he says, if he is still performing at the level he is now by the middle of next year, why not? But as yet it's not clear what Ferrari will think about that.

Hamilton's presence - and the long-term contract held by team-mate Charles Leclerc - does raise questions about Ferrari's driver academy.

First and foremost, those questions surround Oliver Bearman, who is yet to finalise his new contract with Haas for next season.

Bearman has had a strong season and a new deal is believed to be pretty much a formality - driver and team have expressed their desire to stay together, and the Briton was talking in a BBC 5 live interview at the weekend very much as if he would still be a Haas driver next year .…

title: UCI Gravel World Series: Former junior champion steps up to claim elite women's win at a muddy Gravelista while rowing Olympic medallist sails away for elite men's victory
author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
text:
The first 2027 Australian qualifier of the UCI Gravel World Series, Gravelista, crowned two very different first time series winners. The 19-year-old Ruby Taylor claimed the elite women's victory and an Olympic silver medallist in rowing, Great Britain's Harry Leask, won the elite men's category.

They both, however, crossed the line solo in muddy and wet conditions after the race, for a second year, was hit by a cool turn in the spring conditions. That resulted in a shortening of the original 135km course to 97.1km with 1,154m of elevation gain.

Taylor excelled in the conditions to take her first UCI Gravel World Series elite victory in dominating style. The young rider, who won the junior Australian gravel title two years ago, crossed the line after three hours, eight minutes and 36 seconds with a margin of nearly nine minutes to the closest women's competitor, Laura Tomlinson, who was riding in the 19-34 year old age-group category.

The 40-44 rider Belen Lopez Morales, who from 2011-13 claimed the Spanish time trial title on the road, was next over the line and it was then a group of six, including Great Britain's Hayley Simmonds, at nearly 11 minutes that fought for the next places in the overall and the remaining two spots on the elite women's podium.

The 35-39 category rider Philippa Birch won that sprint and then elite women's category riders Karoline Risager Schmidt – who finished in the top 30 at the UCI Gravel World Championships in Nannup – and Amanda Poulsen took the next two positions. In the process, Risager Schmidt and Poulsen also came second and third in the elite category.

For Taylor the top step was the continuation of a year where she hasn't just been easing her way out of the junior ranks, but blasting into a new category with victories that have often left her older and more experienced rivals leagues behind.

The run of successes has crossed disciplines and includes two stage wins at the three-stage ProVelo Super League round of the Tour of Tasmania plus an U23 Australian XCO Mountain Bike title that not only saw her shed her category rivals but also make up the one minute deficit at the start line to nearly all the elite women out on the course, the only exception being elite victor Rebecca Henderson.

In the men's elite race at Gravelista, which started and finished in Seymour in Victoria, the field included former Australian gravel champions Mark O'Brien and Connor Sens as well as past UCI Gravel World Series race winner Tasman Nankervis but Leask had also marked himself out as a potential threat with second at Devils Cardigan earlier this year.

Leask, who after rowing also became a cyclor in the America's Cup, made a crucial early move with Nankervis and O'Brien.

"Another wet and muddy race. Managed to get away 3 up after the main climb at 30k, then was able to get a gap in the last 6/7k to come across the line solo," said Leask in a post on social media .

The British rider crossed the line in two hours, 31 minutes and 16 seconds, which was 23 seconds ahead of second-placed Nankervis.
